recent_posts.title: Microsoft Vibing — capturing screenshots and voice samples without governance
recent_posts.summary: A Microsoft Research Asia team published a tool called Vibing (via Microsoft Store and GitHub) that silently captures screenshots, clipboard contents, microphone audio, and keystrokes, sending them to a Microsoft Azure endpoint with unique per-machine GUIDs — all without user consent or disclosure. The software is signed by a Microsoft employee but disguised as a community open-source project with no actual source code. Its privacy policy falsely claims no third-party data sharing. Microsoft employees linked to the project have ignored developer concerns raised on GitHub. The author identifies multiple privacy and security violations and provides IoCs for detection.

recent_posts.title: What organisations can learn from the record breaking fine over Capita’s ransomware incident
recent_posts.summary: The UK's Information Commissioner's Office fined Capita £14 million for negligent cybersecurity practices following a Black Basta ransomware attack that exposed data from 6 million people. The breach stemmed from an unaddressed Qakbot infection where SOC alerts went unresponded for 58 hours, lateral movement wasn't contained, and years of unpatched Active Directory vulnerabilities enabled privilege escalation. Key failures included understaffed SOC operations that never met internal SLAs, lack of penetration testing for systems with personal data, ignoring repeated pentest findings about domain admin security, and misleading public communications. Organizations should prioritize properly staffed SOCs with achievable targets, default-deny network policies, regular external penetration testing, Active Directory hardening, transparent crisis communications, and honest pre-emptive testing of security controls.

recent_posts.title: CyberSlop — meet the new threat actor, MIT and Safe Security
recent_posts.summary: A cybersecurity researcher critiques a flawed MIT/Safe Security paper claiming 80% of ransomware attacks use generative AI. The paper, which was later quietly removed, lacked evidence and misrepresented threat data. The author argues that real-world ransomware incidents stem from foundational security failures like credential misuse and unpatched systems, not AI. The piece exposes conflicts of interest between academic researchers and security vendors, and calls for practitioners to challenge misleading industry claims that misdirect security priorities.

recent_posts.title: Microsoft builds on Recall with Gaming Copilot — fails basic privacy tests
recent_posts.summary: Microsoft is rolling out Gaming Copilot to Windows 11 users without explicit consent or onboarding. The feature uses AI to capture gameplay screenshots and send data to Azure cloud endpoints for processing, similar to the controversial Recall feature. By default, it trains Microsoft's AI models on user text and screenshots, records conversations, and infers interests for personalization and potential advertising. The feature installs silently even when Copilot has been uninstalled, lacks privacy configuration options, and continues network traffic even when the UI is closed. This raises significant privacy concerns and introduces new attack surfaces to Windows 11 systems.

recent_posts.title: Red Hat Consulting breach exposes 32 million files from 5000 enterprise customers
recent_posts.summary: Red Hat Consulting suffered a major data breach affecting over 5,000 enterprise customers. The extortion group Crimson Collective, allegedly linked to LAPSUS$ members, claims to have stolen 32 million files including consultancy reports, source code, and sensitive credentials for organizations like HSBC, Walmart, and ING Bank. The breach occurred on September 13, 2025, and exposed private certificates, stored credentials, and customer documentation. Impacted organizations should contact Red Hat support to obtain stolen files and implement remediation measures including certificate rotation and credential changes.

recent_posts.title: The Elephant in The Biz: outsourcing of critical IT and cybersecurity functions risks UK economic security
recent_posts.summary: Three major UK companies (Co-op Group, Marks & Spencer, and Jaguar Land Rover) suffered costly ransomware attacks after outsourcing critical IT and cybersecurity functions to TCS. Combined losses approach £1 billion, with JLR's manufacturing shutdown potentially requiring government intervention to support affected suppliers. The analysis explores how cost-cutting through outsourcing creates systemic economic risks, as MSPs become attractive targets due to their shared infrastructure and lower security standards. The piece argues for policy changes including ransom payment bans and stronger cyber resilience requirements for large organizations.

recent_posts.title: Citrix Netscaler backdoors — Part One — May 2025 activity against governments
recent_posts.summary: Security researchers discovered sophisticated backdoors targeting Citrix Netscaler systems across western governments and legal institutions. The attacks exploited a zero-day vulnerability in getAuthenticationRequirements.do to deploy persistent PHP webshells that survive patching. The campaign, likely attributed to Volt Typhoon, used complex attack chains involving Python scripts, AES-encrypted commands, and privilege escalation techniques. Citrix failed to publicly disclose technical details, providing remediation scripts only under NDAs, leaving organizations vulnerable to ongoing espionage activities.

recent_posts.title: Citrix CVE-2025-6543 exploited as zero day since May, enables remote code execution
recent_posts.summary: CVE-2025-6543, a critical Citrix Netscaler vulnerability, has been actively exploited as a zero-day since May 2025, allowing remote code execution through memory overflow attacks. Despite Citrix initially describing it as merely causing denial of service, the vulnerability has led to widespread compromise of government and legal services worldwide, with attackers deploying webshells and maintaining persistent access even after patching. NCSC Netherlands revealed the true scope of the attacks, showing that threat actors exploited client certificate handling to overwrite memory and execute code, while Citrix failed to provide transparent communication about the severity and active exploitation to customers.

recent_posts.title: Colt Technical Services gets ransomware’d via SharePoint initial access— some learning points
recent_posts.summary: Colt Technical Services suffered a ransomware attack by the Warlock group through an unpatched SharePoint server vulnerability (CVE-2025-53770). Despite initial patching, attackers had already installed a webshell for persistent access. The incident highlights critical lessons about transparency in crisis communication, the risks of running on-premises SharePoint, and the importance of attack surface management. The company's delayed disclosure allowed threat actors to leak customer data on dark web forums before proper incident response messaging began.

recent_posts.title: CitrixBleed 2 vulnerability actively exploited by Chinese APT and ransomware groups
recent_posts.summary: CVE-2025-5777 (CitrixBleed 2) has been actively exploited since June 2025 by multiple threat actor groups including Chinese APT groups targeting government and financial sectors, Russian ransomware operators, and widespread e-crime actors. Citrix initially downplayed exploitation but was forced to acknowledge it after CISA added the vulnerability to their Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. The vulnerability affects NetScaler appliances and allows session hijacking, with most organizations lacking sufficient logging to detect compromise. Citrix's patching instructions are incomplete, failing to clear all session cookie types that could still be exploited.
